why.correct: Basal cells at the base of each taste bud are stem cells. Gustatory receptor cells last about a week or two on average, and basal cells divide to make their replacements.
options: Sensory neurons receive signals from the taste cells; they do not divide to make new taste cells.
Correct. Basal cells are the stem cells of the taste bud.
The taste pore is just an opening in the surface. The cells whose microvilli reach into it are the gustatory receptor cells themselves, which wear out rather than replace others.
Supporting cells belong to the olfactory epithelium, not the taste bud, and they support neurons rather than replacing taste cells.

why.correct: Every region of the tongue that has taste buds detects all five taste qualities. The tip has taste buds with salt-sensing cells, so she tastes salt at once. The tongue map, which puts only sweet at the tip, is a myth.
options: Salt triggers the salty quality wherever it lands. Taste buds at the tip are not limited to sweet; that idea comes from the tongue map, which is wrong.
The sides of the tongue are not the only place salt is sensed. Taste buds at the tip detect it directly.
Correct. Na+ enters salt-sensing cells at the tip, and she tastes salt immediately.
Sodium ions trigger the salty quality, not bitter. Bitter compounds act on their own receptor proteins.

why.correct: A blow to the head can jolt the brain against the skull and tear the thin olfactory axons where they pass through the cribriform plate. His taste qualities are intact, so what he has lost is smell, which provides most of what people call flavor.
options: His gustatory receptor cells work: he identifies all four solutions correctly.
Correct. Anosmia after a head injury usually comes from torn olfactory axons at the cribriform plate.
Damage to one facial nerve would reduce taste on the front two thirds of that side of the tongue, but it would not stop him identifying odors by sniffing.
Damage to the gustatory cortex would impair his perception of taste qualities, which is normal. His problem is with odors.

why.correct: An odorant must dissolve in mucus before it can bind a receptor protein. Binding activates a G protein, which switches on the enzyme that makes the second messenger cAMP. cAMP opens cation channels; the calcium that enters opens chloride channels, and Cl− leaving depolarizes the cell further. Once the axon reaches threshold, action potentials pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, and the olfactory tract carries the signal on.

Na+ flowing in carries positive charge into the cell, so it depolarizes. That change in voltage is the taste cell's receptor potential, and it sets how much neurotransmitter the cell releases onto the sensory neuron.
options: Gustatory receptor cells are epithelial cells with no axon. They cannot send action potentials to the medulla; the sensory neuron they contact does that.
Salty taste works through an ion channel: Na+ enters directly. G protein–coupled receptor proteins serve sweet, umami and bitter.
Correct. The inflow of positive charge is the cell's receptor potential.
Basal cells replace worn-out taste cells over days. They play no part in the second-to-second response to salt.

why.correct: Taste relays in the thalamus on its way from the medulla to the gustatory cortex. The olfactory bulb receives only olfactory axons.
options: This step is right. Taste cells are not neurons; they pass the signal to a sensory neuron at a synapse.
This step is right. The facial nerve carries taste from the front two thirds of the tongue.
This step is right. Taste fibers from the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves all end in one nucleus in the medulla.
This is the error. The relay between the medulla and the cortex is the thalamus. The olfactory bulb is part of the smell pathway.
This step is right. The gustatory cortex lies in the insula and the nearby frontal lobe.

why.correct: Olfactory signals go from the olfactory bulb through the olfactory tract straight to the olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe. Every other sense relays in the thalamus before it reaches the cortex.
options: Correct. Only later do some olfactory signals pass through the thalamus to the frontal lobe.
Olfactory signals never enter the spinal cord. They travel from the nose to the brain in the olfactory nerve.
Smell uses cranial nerve I, the olfactory nerve, formed by the bundles of olfactory axons.
Olfactory sensory neurons are neurons with axons, which pass through the cribriform plate. It is the gustatory receptor cells of taste that have no axon.

why.correct: Sweet, umami and bitter tastants bind G protein–coupled receptor proteins, which set off a second messenger cascade. Salty and sour work through ion channels: Na+ and H+ flow straight into the cell.
options: Not this one. Na+ enters directly through sodium channels.
Yes. Sugars bind a G protein–coupled receptor protein.
Not this one. H+ enters directly through a proton channel.
Yes. Glutamate binds a G protein–coupled receptor protein.
Yes. Bitter compounds bind one of about 25 G protein–coupled receptor proteins.

why.correct: Binding is untouched, but every step after the enzyme weakens: less cAMP, fewer open cation channels, less chloride current, a smaller receptor potential and fewer action potentials, so the smell seems faint.

variables.name: Odorant binding to odorant receptor proteins
variables.why: The chemical acts on the enzyme inside the cell, after binding. The odorant still reaches and binds its receptor proteins on the cilia.

variables.name: cAMP made in the cilia
variables.why: The activated G protein cannot switch on a blocked enzyme, so little cAMP is made.

variables.name: Opening of cation channels in the cilia
variables.why: These channels are opened by cAMP, so with less cAMP fewer open and less Na+ and Ca2+ enter.

variables.name: Size of the neuron's receptor potential
variables.why: Less cation entry means less Ca2+ to open chloride channels too, so both parts of the depolarization shrink.

variables.name: Perceived strength of the smell
variables.why: Smaller receptor potentials mean fewer action potentials reach the olfactory bulb and cortex.

why.correct: Most of what people call taste is smell. Odorants rising from food in the mouth normally reach the olfactory epithelium at the top of the nose. A blocked nose stops them, so only the five taste qualities remain and the food seems flat.
options: A cold does not destroy taste cells in the mouth. She would still detect salt or sweetness in the curry.
Nasal mucus does not coat the taste buds in the mouth. Taste pores sit in the saliva-covered surface of the tongue.
A cold does not inflame the facial nerve, and damage to it would affect only taste on the front of the tongue, not the flavor of the whole meal.
Correct. Her taste buds still work; the smell part of flavor is missing.

why.correct: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries taste from the back third of the tongue. The facial nerve carries the front two thirds, and the vagus carries the throat and epiglottis.
options: The facial nerve carries taste from the front two thirds of the tongue, not the back third.
The trigeminal nerve carries touch, temperature and pain from the tongue, not taste.
The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve that moves the tongue. It carries no taste.
Correct. Cranial nerve IX serves taste on the back third of the tongue.

why.correct: Umami is the savory taste of glutamate, an amino acid found in broth, aged cheese and ripe tomatoes, and added to food as monosodium glutamate.
options: Hydrogen ions from acids trigger the sour quality.
Sodium ions trigger the salty quality.
Glucose and other sugars trigger the sweet quality.
Correct. Glutamate binds the umami receptor protein.

why.correct: The olfactory tract connects directly with the limbic system. The amygdala handles emotion and the hippocampus region handles memory, so a smell can call up a memory and its feelings very quickly.
options: Replacement of olfactory neurons explains recovery of smell after damage, not the link between smell and memory.
Correct. Smell has an unusually short route into the limbic structures for emotion and memory.
Olfactory signals reach the cortex without a first relay in the thalamus, so this cannot be the explanation.
Receptor proteins bind odorants; they store no memories. Memory depends on the brain, including the hippocampus.

why.correct: Acids release H+. In sour-sensing taste cells, H+ flows in through a proton channel, carrying positive charge in and depolarizing the cell directly, like Na+ in salty taste.
options: Sour works through an ion channel, not a G protein–coupled receptor protein. The G protein route serves sweet, umami and bitter.
Correct. The inflow of H+ is the depolarizing current.
The chloride current that adds to depolarization belongs to olfactory sensory neurons, not sour-sensing taste cells.
Strong acids can also sting, but the sour taste itself comes from gustatory receptor cells, not nociceptors.

why.correct: Each odorant activates several kinds of receptor protein, some strongly and some weakly, and each receptor protein responds to several odorants. The pattern across all the kinds identifies the odor, the way a chord is identified by its combination of notes.
options: Each olfactory sensory neuron makes just one kind of receptor protein. That is what lets the bulb sort signals by receptor type.
There are far fewer receptor protein kinds than odors, and the set is fixed by your genes. Odors share receptor proteins.
Correct. Odor identity is a pattern across many kinds of receptor protein, not a single kind.
The bulb sorts and pools signals by receptor type; it does not create new ways of detecting odorants.

why.correct: Basal stem cells in the olfactory epithelium divide and produce new olfactory sensory neurons, which grow axons back through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb. Olfactory sensory neurons are among the few neurons replaced throughout life.
options: Correct. They rebuild the epithelium, and smell returns over weeks to months.
Taste bud basal cells replace gustatory receptor cells, not olfactory neurons.
Cortical neurons do not regrow the sensory neurons in the nose.
Supporting cells surround and support the neurons; the new neurons come from the basal stem cells.

why.correct: Olfactory sensory neurons keep chloride unusually high inside. When the channels open, Cl− moves down its gradient out of the cell. Negative charge leaving makes the inside less negative, so the cell depolarizes.
options: Chloride is always a negative ion. What differs is the direction it moves.
Correct. Negative ions leaving make the inside less negative.
These channels pass chloride. Na+ enters through the separate cAMP-gated cation channels.
cAMP opens cation channels; it does not change ion gradients. The chloride gradient is set by how much chloride these neurons accumulate.

why.correct: Capsaicin in chili opens the same heat-sensitive channels that real heat opens, on free nerve endings of the trigeminal nerve. The brain reads their signal as burning. It is not one of the five taste qualities.
options: Sour cells respond to hydrogen ions. Capsaicin does not act through them.
Olfactory neurons detect odorants in the nose; the burn is felt in the mouth by pain-sensing endings.
Bitter cells respond to bitter compounds through their own receptor proteins, not to capsaicin's heat channel.
Correct. The burn is a pain and heat signal, not a taste.

why.correct: More sugar binds more receptor proteins, so the taste cell's receptor potential grows and it releases more neurotransmitter. The sensory neuron then fires action potentials more often. Stimulus strength is coded by frequency.
options: Correct. A bigger receptor potential means more release and a higher firing rate in the sensory neuron.
Action potentials are all-or-none: they do not get bigger. Strength is coded by how often they fire.
Nerves carry electrical signals, not the tastant molecules themselves.
Gustatory receptor cells are epithelial cells with no axon at any stimulus strength. Every taste signal reaches the brain through a sensory neuron.

why.correct: The optic disc is where the ganglion cell axons leave the eye as the optic nerve and the central retinal vessels enter. It has no photoreceptors, so it makes the blind spot.
options: The fovea is the small cone-only pit of sharpest vision, beside the optic disc rather than where the nerve leaves.
The ciliary body is the ring of muscle and folds around the lens at the front of the eye.
Correct. The spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye is the optic disc, the blind spot.
The choroid is the dark, vessel-rich middle layer of the wall, not a spot on the retina.

why.correct: The ciliary muscle is the ring of smooth muscle in the ciliary body. Contracting it slackens the zonule fibers so the lens can round up for near vision.
options: Correct. The muscle in the ciliary body is the ciliary muscle.
The iris is the colored ring in front of the lens, around the pupil.
Zonule fibers are the fine threads running from the ciliary body to the rim of the lens, not the muscle itself.
The scleral venous sinus is the drainage channel for aqueous humor at the angle between the iris and cornea.

why.correct: The optic chiasm is the X-shaped crossing just above the pituitary gland, in front of its stalk, where axons from the nasal half of each retina cross to the other side.
options: The optic tracts run back from the chiasm toward the thalamus; the pinned structure is where the two nerves meet.
The lateral geniculate nucleus is the relay in the thalamus, farther back along the pathway.
The optic nerves run from each eye to the chiasm; the pinned structure is where they meet and cross.
Correct. This is the optic chiasm.

why.correct: The conjunctiva is the thin mucous membrane that covers the white of the eye and lines the inside of the eyelids. It stops at the edge of the cornea.
options: The cornea is the clear dome at the very front. The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye around it, not the cornea itself.
Correct. This thin membrane over the white of the eye is the conjunctiva.
The sclera is the tough white coat itself; the conjunctiva is the thin clear membrane lying on it.
The orbicularis oculi is the ring of muscle inside the eyelids that closes them.

why.correct: Tears are made by the lacrimal gland in the upper outer orbit, swept toward the inner corner by blinking, and drained through the puncta and canaliculi into the lacrimal sac, then down the nasolacrimal duct into the nose.

The superior oblique turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye is turned in toward the nose, which is the position used for reading and going downstairs. Its nerve, the trochlear nerve, has a long course inside the skull and is easily injured by a blow to the head.
options: The inferior rectus also turns the eye down, but most strongly when the eye is turned out, not in.
The lateral rectus turns the eye out; his problem is looking down while turned in.
Correct. Looking down and in depends on the superior oblique, supplied by the trochlear nerve.
The superior rectus turns the eye up, the opposite of the movement he has lost.

why.correct: This is presbyopia. The lens stiffens with age and can no longer round up for near objects, so near vision blurs and the near point moves outward. Distant vision, which needs no accommodation, is unchanged. Convex reading glasses add the missing bending.

variables.name: How much the lens rounds up when the ciliary muscle contracts
variables.why: A stiffer lens does not bulge into a rounder shape when the zonule fibers go slack.

variables.name: Bending of light from the menu
variables.why: A flatter lens refracts light less, so near rays are not bent enough to meet on the retina.

variables.name: Distance to the nearest point she can see sharply
variables.why: With less accommodation available, only objects farther away need little enough bending to focus, so she holds the menu at arm's length.

variables.name: Sharpness of distant objects
variables.why: Distant objects are focused with the lens flat and the ciliary muscle relaxed, which a stiff lens still manages.

why.correct: Near vision needs more bending. Parasympathetic fibers in the oculomotor nerve contract the ring-shaped ciliary muscle, which shrinks toward the lens. The zonule fibers go slack, and the elastic lens rounds up and refracts more.
options: That is what happens when you look from near to far, not far to near.
Taut zonule fibers pull the lens flat, not round. When the ciliary muscle contracts, the fibers slacken.
The cornea does most of the bending, but its shape is fixed. Only the lens changes for near vision.
Correct. Slack zonules let the elastic lens round up.

why.correct: When the ring of ciliary muscle contracts and shrinks, it moves closer to the lens, so the zonule fibers go slack. Slack fibers release the lens, which rounds up.
options: This step is right. Parasympathetic fibers of cranial nerve III drive accommodation.
This step is right. The ciliary muscle is a ring, so contracting makes it smaller.
This is the error. The zonule fibers slacken; taut fibers would flatten the lens.
This step is right. The released lens rounds up because it is elastic.
This step is right. A rounder lens refracts more.

why.correct: Her acuity is 20/60. The top number is her distance from the chart; the bottom number is the distance at which a normal eye can read the smallest row she read. Her letters must be three times larger than a normal eye needs, so her acuity is worse than normal.
options: Correct. 20/60: she must be at 20 feet for letters a normal eye reads from 60 feet.
This reverses the fraction. She stood at 20 feet; 60 is the distance for a normal eye.
A larger bottom number means worse acuity, not better.
A Snellen fraction is not a percentage of vision; it compares viewing distances.

why.correct: In a long eye (myopia), the cornea and lens bring distant light to a focus before it reaches the retina. A concave lens spreads the rays slightly first, which moves the focus back onto the retina.
options: A focus behind the retina is hyperopia, caused by an eye that is too short.
The focus is in front of the retina, but a convex lens would add bending and move it even farther forward.
A long eye puts the focus in front of the retina, not behind it.
Correct. Myopia: focus in front of the retina, corrected with a diverging (concave) lens.

why.correct: Clear near vision with blurred distant vision is myopia, or nearsightedness. It usually appears in childhood as the eyeball grows too long.
options: Presbyopia blurs near vision and appears in middle age, when the lens stiffens.
Hyperopia blurs near objects first; she reads near print easily.
A cataract clouds the lens and blurs everything, near and far, and is rare in children.
Correct. Near is clear, far is blurred: myopia.

why.correct: This is glaucoma. When aqueous humor drains too slowly, the pressure inside the eye rises and damages the axons of retinal ganglion cells where they leave through the optic disc. Those cells die and are not replaced, and the loss usually starts at the edges of the field.
options: The edge of the field is lost because of damage to the axons carrying it, not because rods themselves die.
Correct. Glaucoma is damage to the optic nerve, the axons of retinal ganglion cells.
Clouding of the lens is a cataract, which blurs the whole field rather than stealing its edges.
The ciliary processes make aqueous humor. They are working; the problem is the drainage.

why.correct: The vascular tunic is the middle layer: the choroid at the back, the ciliary body around the lens, and the iris at the front. The sclera and cornea form the fibrous tunic, and the retina is the neural tunic.
options: Yes. The choroid is the vessel-rich, pigmented layer at the back of the eye.
No. The sclera is part of the outer fibrous tunic.
Yes. The ciliary body joins the choroid to the iris.
No. The retina is the inner, neural tunic.
Yes. The iris is the front part of the vascular tunic.
No. The cornea is the clear front of the fibrous tunic.

why.correct: The fovea holds only tightly packed cones. Each foveal cone connects through its own bipolar cell to its own ganglion cell, so its signal reports one tiny spot, and light reaches the cones without passing through the other layers.
options: The fovea has no rods, and rods converge many-to-one onto ganglion cells, which lowers acuity rather than raising it.
The fovea is at the back of the eye, not especially close to the lens; its sharpness comes from its wiring.
Correct. Low convergence and an unobstructed path give the fovea its acuity.
Blood vessels are kept away from the fovea; vessels in front of it would block light.

why.correct: The fovea holds only cones, which need bright light. Rods are absent from the fovea and plentiful around it, and many rods converge onto each ganglion cell, so their weak signals add up. Looking slightly away puts the star's image on rods.
options: Correct. Rods, outside the fovea, detect dim light.
Bright light bleaches pigment, and a faint star is far too dim to do that.
The optic disc lies about 15 degrees toward the nose from the fovea, not at its center.
The fovea contains no rods.

why.correct: Light straightens retinal (photoisomerization), which activates rhodopsin. Rhodopsin switches on transducin, which switches on an enzyme that breaks down cGMP. With less cGMP, the cation channels close, the dark current stops, the rod hyperpolarizes, and its glutamate release falls.
In photoreceptors, light turns a signal off. It lowers cGMP, closes the cation channels that carried the dark current, hyperpolarizes the rod and reduces its glutamate release.

variables.name: cGMP in the outer segment
variables.why: Active rhodopsin switches on transducin, which switches on the enzyme that breaks down cGMP.

variables.name: Number of open cation channels
variables.why: These channels are held open by cGMP, so they close as cGMP falls.

variables.name: Membrane potential (how positive the inside is)
variables.why: With the Na+ inflow cut off while K+ still leaks out, the rod hyperpolarizes from about −40 toward −70 mV.

variables.name: Glutamate release onto bipolar cells
variables.why: A hyperpolarized rod releases less neurotransmitter; the fall in glutamate is the light signal.

why.correct: The open channels let Na+ (and some Ca2+) flow in continuously. This dark current holds the rod at about −40 mV, depolarized enough to release glutamate all the time.
options: Rods produce graded potentials, not action potentials. Retinal ganglion cells are the first cells in the pathway to fire them.
Rhodopsin switches on transducin only after absorbing light.
Correct. The dark current keeps the rod depolarized.
K+ leaks out of cells, not in, and hyperpolarization is what light causes.

why.correct: The short-wavelength cone curve peaks at 420 nm. At that wavelength the rod and other cone curves are far below their peaks.
options: The rod curve peaks near 498 nm and is low at 420 nm.
Correct. Short-wavelength cones peak at 420 nm.
Medium-wavelength cones peak near 534 nm and absorb little at 420 nm.
Long-wavelength cones peak near 564 nm, far from 420 nm.

why.correct: Color is worked out by comparing the responses of cone types with different curves. Rods all have the same pigment, so a dim light of one wavelength and a brighter light of another can produce the same rod response. With nothing to compare, color cannot be told apart.
options: Correct. One pigment gives one curve, and one curve cannot code color.
The rod curve extends well below 500 nm; it simply peaks near 498 nm.
The rod curve rises and falls; it clearly absorbs some wavelengths more than others.
The rod peak, near 498 nm, is blue-green light that many objects reflect.

why.correct: The outer half of each eye's field is seen by the nasal half of each retina. Those are exactly the axons that cross in the middle of the optic chiasm. A pituitary tumor growing up from below typically presses there, causing bitemporal hemianopia.
options: Correct. Crossing fibers from both nasal retinas run through the middle of the chiasm.
A left optic tract lesion removes the right half of the field in both eyes, not the outer half of each.
A right optic nerve lesion blinds the right eye only.
Damage to both occipital lobes would cause far wider loss; a single mass pressing on one structure fits the chiasm.

why.correct: Behind the chiasm, the right optic tract carries the temporal fibers of the right eye and the crossed nasal fibers of the left eye. Both see the left side of the world, so the left half of the field is lost in both eyes: a left homonymous hemianopia.
options: Blindness in one eye comes from damage to that eye's optic nerve, before the chiasm.
Loss of both outer halves comes from damage to the crossing fibers in the middle of the chiasm.
The right half of the field is carried by the left optic tract.
Correct. Each optic tract carries the opposite half of the visual field from both eyes.

why.correct: When the right eye is lit, both pupils narrow, so both efferent paths (both oculomotor nerves and both iris sphincters) work. When the left eye is lit, nothing happens, so the signal never gets in: the afferent path from the left eye, the left optic nerve, is damaged.
options: A left oculomotor lesion would leave the left pupil wide whichever eye is lit, but here it narrows when the right eye is lit.
A right oculomotor lesion would stop the right pupil narrowing, but it narrows when the right eye is lit.
Correct. Light in the damaged eye cannot start the reflex; light in the healthy eye drives both pupils.
The chiasm has no separate "right" half for one eye's pupil fibers, and damage there would not silence one eye's input completely.

why.correct: Narrowing of the pupil is miosis. It is caused by contraction of the circular sphincter muscle of the iris, which is supplied by parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve.
options: Mydriasis is widening of the pupil, and sympathetic fibers widen it.
Mydriasis means a wide pupil, not a narrow one.
Correct. Miosis is a narrow pupil, driven by parasympathetic fibers.
The pupil is narrowed by parasympathetic fibers; sympathetic fibers act on the dilator fibers and widen it.

why.correct: The ventral stream, running from the occipital lobe forward into the temporal lobe, identifies what things are, including faces. His ability to locate and grasp the cup shows that the dorsal stream still works.
options: The dorsal stream guides reaching and locating, which he does well.
Damage to the lateral geniculate nucleus would cause loss of part of the visual field, not a loss of recognition with normal reaching.
Chiasm damage causes field loss, typically the outer halves, not a loss of object recognition.
Correct. Recognizing objects and faces is the job of the ventral "what" stream.

why.correct: The genes for the medium- and long-wavelength pigments sit on the X chromosome. A male has one X, so one faulty copy changes his color vision. A female usually has a working copy on her second X.
options: Males and females have similar numbers of cones.
Correct. One X chromosome means one copy of the pigment genes.
The condition is present from birth and does not come from hormones damaging pigments.
Rod and cone numbers do not differ this way between the sexes, and rods do not cause color blindness.

why.correct: The only step in vision that needs light is photoisomerization: the bent 11-cis-retinal straightens into all-trans-retinal. The change of shape activates the opsin around it.
options: Correct. Photoisomerization is the light-driven step.
Opsin does not break down cGMP; it switches on transducin, which switches on the enzyme that does.
Light closes the cation channels; cGMP holds them open in the dark.
Retinal goes to the pigmented epithelium later, after it has come away from the opsin, not at the moment of absorption.

why.correct: Light is refracted first by the cornea and then by the lens, and is absorbed by the photoreceptors at the back of the retina. The signal passes through bipolar and ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve, cross (the nasal ones) at the optic chiasm, run in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate nucleus and reach the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
The incus is the middle ossicle. It links the malleus, attached to the eardrum, to the stapes in the oval window.
options: The malleus is the ossicle attached to the inside of the eardrum, the first in the chain.
The stapes is the last ossicle, whose footplate sits in the oval window.
Correct. The middle bone of the chain is the incus.
The tympanic membrane is the sheet stretched across the end of the ear canal, not a bone.

why.correct: The auditory (eustachian) tube runs from the middle ear down to the upper throat behind the nose. It opens when you swallow and equalizes the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
options: The ear canal runs from the outside to the eardrum, on the other side of the middle ear.
Correct. This is the auditory tube, also called the eustachian tube.
The cochlear nerve leaves the cochlea toward the brainstem; it is not a tube to the throat.
The semicircular canals are the looped channels of the inner ear, above the cochlea.

why.correct: The basilar membrane forms the floor of the cochlear duct and carries the spiral organ. Sound makes it vibrate, which bends the hair cells' stereocilia.
options: The tectorial membrane is the gel flap lying over the hair cells, above them rather than beneath.
The tympanic membrane is the eardrum, in the ear canal, not inside the cochlea.
The scala tympani is the lower fluid channel, below the membrane that is pinned.
Correct. The floor of the cochlear duct under the spiral organ is the basilar membrane.

why.correct: The cupula is the tall gel cap in the ampulla of a semicircular canal. The stereocilia of the hair cells project into it, and flowing endolymph bends it when the head turns.
options: Correct. The gel cap spanning the ampulla is the cupula.
The otolithic membrane is the crystal-topped gel over a macula in the utricle or saccule, not in a semicircular canal.
A macula is the patch of hair cells in the utricle or saccule.
The tectorial membrane lies over the hair cells of the cochlea, not the semicircular canals.

why.correct: The eardrum vibrates, the ossicles pass the vibration to the oval window, the stapes sets up waves in the perilymph, the basilar membrane vibrates, and the tectorial membrane slides across the hair cells and bends their stereocilia.

Cochlear nerve fibers synapse in the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem. Signals then reach the superior olivary nuclei on both sides, where the two ears are compared, climb to the inferior colliculus of the midbrain, relay in the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and arrive at the primary auditory cortex.
Fluid in the middle ear causes a conductive hearing loss: sound in the air reaches the cochlea poorly, but sound through bone reaches it normally. The Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear.

variables.name: Movement of the tympanic membrane in response to sound
variables.why: Fluid behind the eardrum resists its movement, so it vibrates less for the same sound.

variables.name: Vibration passed along the ossicles to the oval window
variables.why: The ossicles are damped by the fluid and driven by a stiffer eardrum, so less vibration reaches the oval window.

variables.name: Quietest sound heard through the air (hearing threshold)
variables.why: Less of each sound reaches the cochlea, so a sound must be louder before it is heard.

variables.name: Response of the cochlea to a tuning fork pressed on the skull
variables.why: Bone conduction shakes the cochlea directly, bypassing the middle ear, and the cochlea itself is healthy.

variables.name: Loudness in the left ear of a tuning fork placed on the forehead
variables.why: In the Weber test, a conductive loss makes the fork sound louder in the affected ear, because room noise no longer masks it there.

why.correct: High frequencies vibrate the narrow, stiff base of the basilar membrane most, close to the oval window. Low frequencies travel farther and peak near the wide, floppy apex. Which hair cells are stimulated tells the brain the pitch.
options: The wide, floppy apex vibrates most for low frequencies, not high ones.
Each frequency makes the traveling wave peak at one place; the membrane does not vibrate equally along its length.
Correct. High pitch is coded near the base.
The round window is where the scala tympani ends at the middle ear; the basilar membrane lies along the cochlear duct.

why.correct: Normal Rinne tests rule out a conductive block, so this is sensorineural. High frequencies are sensed near the base of the cochlea, and noise damages hair cells there first, especially the outer hair cells.
options: Correct. Noise-induced loss is sensorineural and starts at the high-frequency base.
Damaged ossicles would cause a conductive loss, with bone conduction better than air in the Rinne test.
The apex senses low frequencies, which he still hears.
Each ear sends signals to both hemispheres, and cortical damage would not give a frequency-specific loss like this.

why.correct: Bending toward the tallest stereocilium stretches the tip links, which pull mechanically gated channels open. K+ from the endolymph flows in and depolarizes the cell, which then releases more glutamate onto its sensory neuron.
options: This is what happens when the bundle bends away from the tallest stereocilium.
Correct. Toward the tallest: channels open and the cell depolarizes.
Hair cells have no axon. They release neurotransmitter onto sensory neurons, which fire the action potentials.
K+ flows in, not out, because the endolymph around the stereocilia is rich in K+ and positively charged.

why.correct: The tips of the stereocilia are bathed in endolymph, which is high in K+ and held about 80 mV positive to the perilymph. Both the chemical and electrical gradients push K+ into the cell when the channels open.
options: Correct. The unusual fluid around the stereocilia reverses the usual K+ flow.
Hair cells, like other cells, hold plenty of K+ inside; the difference is the K+-rich, positive fluid outside the stereocilia.
The channels are passive, mechanically gated channels; ions move down their gradients without ATP.
K+ is always a positive ion.

why.correct: Stretched tip links pull mechanically gated channels open. K+ from the endolymph flows in and depolarizes the cell.
options: Correct. Opening mechanically gated channels is the transduction step.
Hair cells do not fire action potentials; their sensory neurons do.
The tectorial membrane is a gel with no cells that release transmitter; it bends the stereocilia as it slides across the hair cells.
Otoliths belong to the maculae of the vestibule, not the cochlea.

why.correct: Hair cells are epithelial sensory receptor cells with no axon. They release glutamate onto the endings of spiral ganglion neurons, and it is those neurons whose axons form the cochlear nerve.
options: This step is right. Vibration of the basilar membrane bends the stereocilia.
This step is right. Bending opens mechanically gated channels.
This is the error. Hair cells have no axons; they pass the signal across a synapse.
This step is right. More glutamate release makes the sensory neurons fire faster.
This step is right. Cochlear nerve fibers synapse in the cochlear nuclei.

why.correct: Bone conduction beating air conduction on the right means sound is blocked on its way through the right external or middle ear: a conductive loss. The Weber test fits, because a conductive loss makes the fork louder in the affected ear.
options: A right sensorineural loss would send the Weber sound to the left ear, and air conduction would still beat bone on the right.
Correct. Weber to the right plus bone better than air on the right means a right conductive loss.
A left sensorineural loss would also send the Weber sound right, but it would not make bone beat air in the right Rinne test.
A left conductive loss would send the Weber sound to the left ear.

why.correct: A Weber result lateralized to the right means either a right conductive loss or a left sensorineural loss. Air better than bone on both sides rules out a conductive block. So the left cochlea or cochlear nerve is damaged, and the sound goes to the better, right ear.
options: A right conductive loss would make bone conduction beat air in the right Rinne test.
A left conductive loss would send the Weber sound to the left, not the right.
With normal hearing, the Weber sound is heard in the middle.
Correct. Weber toward the good ear with normal Rinne tests points to sensorineural loss in the other ear.

why.correct: A fixed stapes cannot pass vibration from the ossicles into the cochlea, so sound through the air is blocked in the middle ear: a conductive loss. Bone conduction reaches the healthy cochlea directly, so it is heard better than air.
options: The cochlea and nerve are healthy; the block is in the middle ear, so the loss is conductive.
In a conductive loss, air conduction is the route that is blocked, so it is no longer better than bone.
Correct. A middle ear block is conductive, and bone beats air in the Rinne test.
In a sensorineural loss both routes are reduced and air still beats bone; here the cochlea is healthy.

why.correct: A louder sound has a larger amplitude. The basilar membrane moves farther, each hair cell bends more and releases more glutamate, so its sensory neurons fire faster, and the peak spreads to recruit more hair cells.
options: The place of the peak codes pitch, which has not changed.
Correct. Loudness is coded by firing rate and the number of neurons recruited.
Inner hair cells carry nearly all the signal to the brain at every loudness; outer hair cells mainly amplify.
Action potentials are all-or-none; they do not grow with stimulus strength.

why.correct: During descent the cabin air pressure rises above the pressure trapped in the middle ear, so the eardrum bows inward and vibrates poorly. Swallowing opens the auditory tube, air enters the middle ear, and the pressures equalize.
options: The auditory tube connects the middle ear to the throat, not to the ear canal, and swallowing opens it.
The stapes stays in the oval window; the problem is the pressure difference across the eardrum.
The cochlea is sealed in bone and is not connected to the auditory tube.
Correct. Equal pressure lets the eardrum vibrate freely again.

why.correct: Auditory fibers cross at several levels, beginning at the superior olivary nuclei, so each ear reaches both auditory cortices. Losing one cortex does not deafen either ear, although locating sounds and understanding speech can suffer.
options: Unlike touch, hearing from each ear reaches both hemispheres, so one-sided cortical damage does not deafen the opposite ear.
The left ear also sends signals to the intact right cortex.
Correct. Bilateral pathways protect against deafness from one-sided cortical damage.
Frequency is mapped across each auditory cortex; losing one side does not remove high pitches from both ears.

why.correct: Up-and-down linear acceleration is sensed mainly by the saccule, whose macula stands vertical. As the lift accelerates upward, the heavy, crystal-topped gel lags and bends the stereocilia.
options: Correct. The vertical macula of the saccule senses vertical movement.
The horizontal macula of the utricle senses forward, backward and sideways movement and head tilt.
The semicircular canals sense turning, not straight-line movement.
The cochlear duct is part of the hearing organ, not the vestibular apparatus.

why.correct: During steady spinning, the endolymph catches up with the canal and the cupula returns upright. When she stops, the fluid's inertia keeps it flowing, which bends the cupula the opposite way and signals a turn in the other direction.
options: Loose otoliths cause brief positional dizziness, not the normal after-spin sensation everyone feels.
Correct. The lagging fluid now overshoots and bends the cupula the other way.
The cupula has the same density as endolymph and no crystals, so gravity does not pull it.
Nerve fatigue would reduce firing, not create a clear sense of turning in a particular direction.

why.correct: The vestibular apparatus is the vestibule, with the utricle and saccule, and the three semicircular canals. The basilar membrane and scala vestibuli belong to the cochlea, and the tympanic membrane to the external ear.
options: Yes. The utricle senses tilt and horizontal movement.
No. The basilar membrane is in the cochlea and serves hearing.
Yes. The saccule senses vertical movement.
Yes. The semicircular canals sense turning.
No. The tympanic membrane is the eardrum, at the end of the ear canal.
No. Despite its name, the scala vestibuli is a channel of the cochlea.

why.correct: The semicircular canals signal the head turn to the vestibular nuclei, which drive the eye muscles to turn both eyes the same amount in the opposite direction. The image stays still on the retinas and the sign stays sharp.
options: Turning the eyes with the head would make the image slide across the retinas, the opposite of what the reflex does.
The reflex moves both eyes together, keeping them aligned.
Without the reflex the image would slide and blur; the reflex prevents this.
Correct. The eyes counter-rotate to hold the image steady.

why.correct: The force collected over the large eardrum is delivered onto the small footplate. Pressure is force divided by area, so the pressure at the oval window rises about 17-fold, plus a little more from the lever of the ossicles. That boost lets sound pass from air into fluid instead of bouncing off.
options: Correct. Concentrating force onto a small area raises pressure.
The middle ear does not change a sound's frequency; the pitch you hear is the pitch that arrived.
The area ratio raises pressure. Protection from loud sound comes from two small muscles that stiffen the ossicles.
The eardrum drives the ossicles; the area difference works through them.

why.correct: Fluid cannot be squeezed into a smaller volume. When the stapes pushes the oval window in, the pressure wave travels through the perilymph and pushes the membrane of the round window out into the middle ear, which lets the fluid, and the basilar membrane, move.
options: The inner ear holds fluid, not air, and the stapes sits in the oval window.
Correct. The round window is the pressure release for the incompressible fluid.
The round window opens from the scala tympani into the middle ear, not to the semicircular canals.
The round window is sealed by a membrane; no fluid drains through it.
